projects.title: Anduril Industries AI Grand Prix
projects.summary: Built a fully autonomous drone racing pilot for the Anduril Industries AI Grand Prix: MAVLink comms, computer vision gate detection, state estimation, cascade controllers, and a system ID study to inform the control design.
projects.description:
**What** — A fully autonomous drone pilot stack built for the Anduril Industries AI Grand Prix competition, designed to navigate a racing course from takeoff to landing without any human input.

**How** — Developed MAVLink communication handlers for telemetry and command, a computer vision pipeline for gate detection, state estimation (Kalman Filter on IMU+CV data), and a cascade controller architecture managing thrust and attitude. Conducted a system identification study of the drone's flight dynamics to help guide control design.

**Results** — Advanced to the final round of virtual qualifiers, but did not make it to physical competition. The system achieves stable autonomous flight with real-time gate detection and course navigation.

**Challenges** — The simulator registered drone thrust as a series of large, isolated impulses rather than a smooth continuous force, making raw IMU-based velocity estimation extremely noisy and unreliable. A buffer-based smoothing approach was implemented to manage the impulses, and a system identification study of the thrust characteristics was attempted to better model the dynamics. Ultimately, combining IMU estimates with computer vision measurements was necessary to get reliable velocity and state estimates.

A separate and more disruptive issue involved the simulator's interpretation of MAVLink commands. Bitmask 7 is documented to set a desired attitude target while ignoring angular rate inputs, but the simulator consistently treated it as an angular rate command instead. A full controls architecture was built around that behavior, only for the simulator to silently switch its interpretation to match the official documentation partway through the competition. This effectively invalidated a large portion of the controls work already done. The controls were rebuilt to align with the corrected behavior.

projects.title: Embedded GPS-Aided Navigation System
projects.summary: Built a real-time GPS-aided navigation system from scratch on an ESP32-S3: a hand-implemented Madgwick AHRS filter and 9-state linear Kalman filter fusing 100 Hz IMU data with 4 Hz GPS to estimate position, velocity, and orientation in embedded C++ without any matrix libraries.
projects.description:
**What** — A from-scratch inertial navigation system on an ESP32-S3 microcontroller, fusing high-rate IMU data with low-rate GPS to produce real-time estimates of position, velocity, and orientation. All filter algorithms are implemented by hand in embedded C++, without any external matrix libraries.

**How** — A two-stage architecture keeps the system fully linear. The first stage runs a Madgwick AHRS filter to track orientation as a quaternion, fusing gyroscope integration with accelerometer-based gravity correction and GPS course bearing for yaw at speed. The second stage runs a 9-state linear Kalman filter (position, velocity, and accelerometer bias per axis) that uses the Madgwick quaternion to rotate body-frame accelerations into world-frame ENU coordinates before integrating them. GPS provides absolute position corrections at 4 Hz, and a Zero Velocity Update (ZUPT) is triggered during stationary periods to prevent velocity error from accumulating freely. Sensor calibration runs at startup: 500 IMU samples average out gyro bias, and 50 GPS fixes establish the ENU origin. A Python telemetry script renders a live 3D visualization of both orientation and position simultaneously.

**Results** — When stationary, the Kalman position estimate converges to within roughly 1 meter of the starting point. Pitch and roll from the Madgwick filter are solid with no observable drift. Yaw drifts slowly without a magnetometer, corrected only during GPS movement above 2 m/s. The system is genuinely useful for smooth trajectory logging, short-gap dead reckoning across brief GPS outages, and attitude monitoring. Sub-10-meter dynamic tracking is a hardware limitation of the consumer GPS noise floor, not a filter design limitation.

**Challenges** — Electromagnetic interference was a practical concern from the start. The MPU6050 runs I2C at high speed and is sensitive to common-mode noise picked up by the wiring. Braiding the wires to the IMU provided a meaningful reduction in accelerometer noise and was a simple but important hardware fix.

A bug in the IMU timestamp initialized the time at boot rather than after the startup calibration. This created a massive initial 'dt' that corrupted the Madgwick filter's orientation quaternion, causing the Kalman filter to miscalculate gravity and introduce significant position drift. The issue was resolved by simply recording the initial timestamp exactly when the first sensor sample is actually read.

projects.title: 3DoF Plane System Identification Study
projects.summary: Implemented and validated NASA's SIDPAC system identification framework against a custom Python 3-DoF flight dynamics engine, achieving sub-5% parameter estimation error under noisy, disturbed conditions.
projects.description:
**What** — A research study evaluating system identification methods for 3-DoF aerodynamic models under noisy and data-limited conditions representative of real flight test environments.

**How** — Reviewed existing literature and implemented NASA's SIDPAC system identification framework. Built a custom Python-based 3-DoF flight dynamics engine to generate controlled, high-fidelity datasets, then used it to simulate eight targeted edge-case scenarios under external disturbances, enabling systematic evaluation of estimator performance across degraded data conditions.

**Results** — Achieved sub-5% parameter estimation error in noisy 3-DoF aerodynamic simulations with external disturbances using the SIDPAC approach. The custom simulation engine improved testing reliability and provided a repeatable benchmark environment for comparing identification methods.

**Challenges** — The core 3-DoF equation structure was relatively well-defined given the standardized aerodynamic formulations available in literature, so implementing the baseline simulator and system identification workflow was smooth. The more difficult part was augmenting the simulation with realistic degradations like atmospheric gust disturbances and actuator delay. Once integrated, these disturbances introduced enough additional dynamics that the SIDPAC parameter estimator began struggling to converge consistently. Several variations were attempted to model these effects more faithfully in the parameter estimation process, including explicit actuator delay modeling and gust shaping, but reliable convergence under the more aggressive combined conditions proved elusive. This points to a genuine limitation of the approach: more sophisticated algorithms, such as multi-shot versions or frequency-domain analysis, may be better suited to these conditions and would be a natural next direction for the study.

projects.title: Acoustic Drone Detection System
projects.summary: Built a fully offline acoustic drone detector in 36 hours: a custom circuit, real-time FFT on an ESP32, and an embedded PyTorch model achieving 85% detection accuracy at 15 yards.
projects.description:
**What** — A low-cost, fully standalone acoustic early-warning sensor for nearby drone detection, designed to operate entirely offline with no cloud or internet dependency.

**How** — Repurposed an 8Ω speaker as a directional microphone through a custom breadboarded circuit. Programmed an ESP32 microcontroller in C++ to perform real-time FFT analysis on the incoming audio stream, driving hardware alerts with zero latency. Trained a PyTorch neural network on drone acoustic signatures, then embedded the quantized model weights directly onto the microcontroller for on-device inference.

**Results** — Achieved 85% drone detection accuracy at 15 yards. The complete system (from circuit design through trained model deployment) was built in 36 hours.

**Challenges** — No dedicated microphone was available during the build, and the off-the-shelf sound detector modules on hand performed poorly at the frequency range characteristic of drone motor noise. The workaround was repurposing a speaker as a directional microphone by building a custom amplifier and filtering circuit around it, which gave usable sensitivity in the right frequency band. Getting a clean signal was another significant problem: the improvised microphone picked up ambient noise aggressively and the raw input was very noisy. Rather than trying to solve this entirely in the signal processing layer, the noise robustness was largely offloaded to the neural network itself. Training on noisy samples meant the model learned to ignore the irrelevant frequency content and focus on the drone signature, which turned out to be an effective approach given the hardware constraints and the 36-hour timeline.
